plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 18: Representative Metals, Metalloids, and Nonmetals
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a ball-and-stick model of one tetraphosphorus trisulfide molecule, P4S3, drawn against a plain white background with no axes or scale. Four orange spheres labeled "P" and three smaller yellow spheres labeled "S" are joined by cylindrical bonds colored in halves, orange on the phosphorus end and yellow on the sulfur end. Three phosphorus atoms form a triangular base across the lower part of the model, drawn in perspective with one sphere at the left, one at the right, and one nearer the viewer at the bottom center; solid orange bonds connect all three directly to one another. A fourth phosphorus sits alone at the apex. Each sulfur bridges that apical phosphorus down to one basal phosphorus, placing the sulfurs at the left, right, and middle of the model, the central one drawn in front with its bond running straight down to the near basal atom. The whole is a closed cage in which every sulfur is two-coordinate and every phosphorus three-coordinate. Splitting each bond into two colors keeps the phosphorus-sulfur links distinct and leaves the three phosphorus-phosphorus bonds around the base unmistakable — direct P-P bonding of the kind that gives phosphorus an oxidation state unusual for a group 15 element.

elements: apical phosphorus sphere (orange) labeled P at top center
left basal phosphorus sphere (orange) labeled P
right basal phosphorus sphere (orange) labeled P
front/near basal phosphorus sphere (orange) labeled P at bottom center, drawn larger and lower
left sulfur sphere (yellow, slightly smaller) labeled S
right sulfur sphere (yellow) labeled S
central sulfur sphere (yellow) labeled S, drawn in front between apex and front P
three solid-orange P-P cylindrical bonds forming the basal triangle (left-right, left-front, right-front)
three P-S bonds from apical P down to each S (orange half at P end, yellow half at S end)
three P-S bonds from each S down to its basal P (yellow half at S end, orange half at P end)
per-atom text labels showing element symbol P or S (default overlay)
per-atom text labels showing coordination number 3 (P) or 2 (S) (alternate overlay)

interactions.teaches: Clicking any basal P-P bond lights up all three direct phosphorus-phosphorus bonds, while clicking any P-S bridge lights up all six phosphorus-sulfur links — making the unusual direct P-P bonding visually distinct from the P-S bridges

interactions.label: Labels
interactions.teaches: Switching to coordination numbers shows every sulfur is 2-coordinate and every phosphorus is 3-coordinate, confirming the closed cage connectivity

demo_steps.title: Element symbols
demo_steps.narration: The default view labels each sphere with its element: four orange P and three yellow S. Click a basal P-P bond to highlight the three direct phosphorus-phosphorus bonds of the base triangle.

demo_steps.title: Coordination numbers
demo_steps.narration: Labels become coordination numbers: each S reads 2 (bridging apex P to one basal P) and each P reads 3 (apex P to three S; each basal P to two P and one S).

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: P sphere radius ~0.32 (#e8701a), S sphere radius ~0.27 (#d8d82a). Approximate atom positions: P_apex (0, 1.3, 0.2); P_left (-1.1, -0.5, 0.0); P_right (1.1, -0.5, 0.0); P_front (0, -1.1, 0.9) (nearer +Z so it reads larger/lower); S_left (-1.0, 0.45, 0.1); S_right (1.0, 0.45, 0.1); S_center (0, 0.1, 0.6). Bond cylinder radius ~0.09. P-P bonds (left-right, left-front, right-front) are single solid orange cylinders. Each P-S bond is TWO half-cylinders meeting at the bond midpoint: orange (#e8701a) on the P side, yellow (#d8d82a) on the S side. Bonds: apex-S_left, apex-S_right, apex-S_center, S_left-P_left, S_right-P_right, S_center-P_front. Overall span X ±1.4, Y -1.4..1.6, Z 0..1.0. Labels black, billboarded to camera. Highlight color for selected bond type: bright cyan/white emissive glow; dim non-selected bonds to ~0.35 opacity.
interactionPlan.notes: Build each atom as a MeshSphere with MeshPhongMaterial for the shaded-ball look; bonds as cylinders oriented via quaternion setFromUnitVectors between atom centers. For half-colored P-S bonds place two cylinders each spanning half the segment. Use raycasting on bond meshes for the click interaction; on click, set the bond-type group (P-P vs P-S) emissive and fade the other group. Keep both label sprite sets in the scene and toggle visibility rather than rebuilding text. Add subtle ambient + directional light to reproduce the soft top-left shading of the source spheres.

authoredContext:
The phosphorus distills out of the furnace and is condensed into a solid or burned to form P4O10. The preparation of many other phosphorus compounds begins with P4O10. The acids and phosphates are useful as fertilizers and in the chemical industry. Other uses are in the manufacture of special alloys such as ferrophosphorus and phosphor bronze. Phosphorus is important in making pesticides, matches, and some plastics. Phosphorus is an active nonmetal. In compounds, phosphorus usually occurs in oxidation states of 3−, 3+, and 5+. Phosphorus exhibits oxidation numbers that are unusual for a group 15 element in compounds that contain phosphorus-phosphorus bonds; examples include diphosphorus tetrahydride, H2P-PH2, and tetraphosphorus trisulfide, P4S3, illustrated in the figure.

P4S3 is a component of the heads of strike-anywhere matches.

A ball-and-stick model is shown. Three orange atoms labeled “P” are single bonded together in a triangle shape. Each “P” is single bonded to yellow atoms labeled “S,” which are each single bonded to one other orange atom labeled “P.”

Four orange spheres labeled "P" and three smaller yellow spheres labeled "S" are joined by cylindrical bonds colored in halves, orange on the phosphorus end and yellow on the sulfur end. Three phosphorus atoms form a triangular base across the lower part of the model, drawn in perspective with one sphere at the left, one at the right, and one nearer the viewer at the bottom center; solid orange bonds connect all three directly to one another. A fourth phosphorus sits alone at the apex. Each sulfur bridges that apical phosphorus down to one basal phosphorus, placing the sulfurs at the left, right, and middle of the model, the central one drawn in front with its bond running straight down to the near basal atom. The whole is a closed cage in which every sulfur is two-coordinate and every phosphorus three-coordinate. Splitting each bond into two colors keeps the phosphorus-sulfur links distinct and leaves the three phosphorus-phosphorus bonds around the base unmistakable — direct P-P bonding of the kind that gives phosphorus an oxidation state unusual for a group 15 element.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click a P-P base bond or a P-S bridge to highlight all bonds of that type, making clear that the molecule contains direct phosphorus-phosphorus bonding as well as phosphorus-sulfur links.
- Toggle between atom-count and coordination overlays: labels switch from P/S symbols to coordination numbers, making clear that each sulfur is two-coordinate while each phosphorus is three-coordinate.
